title: Terms
text: Three keys · Step 1 of 16 Terms ← Home Step 1 of 16 · Terms 2 · Before you begin → Time 10 min Difficulty Easy Steps 12 terms You will need: Nothing, just read The words you need before the work begins. Use these definitions as a reference throughout the guide. No secrets are needed to search. Find a term 12 terms shown. Seed phrase A human-readable backup used to derive wallet keys. Keep it secret. Recovery may also require a passphrase and, for multisig, the wallet configuration. Passphrase An additional secret used with a BIP39 seed phrase to derive a different wallet. The exact value matters: a typo can open a different, empty wallet. It is not the device PIN. Entropy Unpredictable input used to generate keys. Correct dice collection can provide entropy; it does not protect against malicious software that handles the result. BIP39 A specification for encoding entropy and a checksum as a mnemonic and deriving a seed from it, with an optional passphrase. It is more than a word list. Airgap Separation from networks. In this guide, secret-handling sessions use verified offline software. Turning networking off does not prove the computer is free of malware. Hash · file fingerprint A digest used to detect file changes. A match is useful only if the expected value comes from a trustworthy source; an attacker can replace both a file and its published hash. Digital signature A cryptographic check that a file was signed by a particular key and has not changed. Verify the signer’s key fingerprint independently; “Good signature” alone does not identify a trustworthy author. Extended public key · xpub Public information that can derive a branch of wallet addresses. It does not authorize spending on its own, but revealing it can expose wallet activity. Wallet descriptor A description of the scripts and public-key information used by a wallet. A watch-only descriptor is not a signing secret, but it is privacy-sensitive and important for multisig recovery. 2-of-3 multisig A wallet policy requiring signatures from two of three keys. Recovering with two seeds also needs the missing cosigner’s public information and the correct policy. PSBT Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction: a format for carrying transaction details and signatures between wallet software and signers. It can be used with single-signature and multisig wallets. Watch-only wallet A wallet holding public information so it can display addresses and transactions. It cannot sign by itself. Verify its receive addresses against independently trusted wallet details. Try the 2-of-3 quorum demo Choose a capability to set up an example, or select individual keys and the wallet map to see what they enable. Signing keys A B C Locked Wallet map The saved public descriptor contains the information needed to recreate wallet addresses. Signing Needs two keys Watch-only Needs wallet map Full recovery Needs backups Signing Locked · Choose two keys. Wallet recovery Select keys or add the wallet map. Reset all Illustration only. Rebuilding from three original seeds requires the original wallet settings. Verify a known receive address before relying on a rebuilt wallet. Independent verification: two matching tools are not enough if both rely on the same compromised input. Check the source of the data as well as the result. Specifications: BIP39 · PSBT (BIP174) . ← Home ← Previous Home Step 1 of 16 2 · Before you begin → Next → Before you begin

title: Before you begin
text: Three keys · Step 2 of 16 Before you begin Plebum Dominium teaches self-custody without a hardware wallet. Create and verify keys with offline software, put the backups on metal, and check that they restore the intended wallet. Use offline software to sign. Hardware wallets are optional signing tools introduced only after the metal backups are complete and checked. ← 1 · Terms Step 2 of 16 · Before you begin 3 · Pick your path → Time 5 min Difficulty Easy Steps 1 worksheet You will need: Pen and paper What are you protecting your Bitcoin from? Two quick questions help you identify your risks. No secret keys or personal information are collected. 1 Choose your concerns ✓ Theft Someone gets access to a backup. ✓ Fire or flood A backup location is destroyed. ✓ Mistakes I lose or record something incorrectly. ✓ Scams Someone tricks me into sharing a secret. ✓ Inheritance My family needs to recover my Bitcoin. 2 Where is your Bitcoin today? On an exchange Someone else controls the keys. Phone or software wallet My keys are on an internet-connected device. Hardware wallet I already use a dedicated signing device. I haven't started I want to begin correctly. Your security priorities Select the risks you want to plan for, then choose where your Bitcoin is today. These choices help you think through risks; they do not automatically determine a safe wallet configuration. Choose your path → Explore wallet risks and tradeoffs One key and a passphrase Simpler to operate, but forgetting or losing the passphrase can permanently prevent recovery. A compromised device or poorly stored backup can still put funds at risk. Keep the passphrase on paper apart from the plate. If someone finds both the seed backup and its passphrase, they may be able to access your funds. Keep them separately and test restoration. A compromised computer or wallet program can expose the key. Offline Mode and fresh boots do not repair compromised hardware or firmware. Restore the seed and exact passphrase in verified offline wallet software. Never enter them into a website, connected computer or support message. Compare several full receiving addresses with independently checked offline wallet records before accepting test coins. The watch-only wallet cannot sign. Spending requires the signing key for the passphrase-protected wallet; recovery requires the seed and the exact passphrase. Compatible offline software can restore the wallet; the original computer or a hardware wallet is not required. Three keys (2-of-3 multisig) Keeps three distinct signing keys in separate records and locations, with two needed to spend. Three keys do not mean three hardware wallets. Setup and recovery require more checks. Securely preserve the wallet configuration/descriptor and test the recovery procedure. Most steps to get right. A missed step in any key can lock the wallet later. If fewer than two signing keys remain available, you cannot spend, even with the wallet map. Losing the map can also prevent recovery when the missing public-key information cannot be reconstructed. Keep three plates in three places, and keep the encrypted map apart from any single plate. Two signing keys meet the 2-of-3 threshold, but recovery also requires the correct wallet configuration. Keep verified copies of the descriptor and recovery instructions in separate safe locations, and rehearse reconstruction and spending before funding the wallet. No passphrase on the 2-of-3. The protection comes from three keys in three places, not from a passphrase. Use a disposable test wallet to practice spending and recovery for your chosen setup. Resolve failures before relying on an intended wallet; a practice transaction alone does not verify its backups. Shut down fully between keys. A key left in memory is a key at risk. Note: One stolen seed being insufficient applies to an appropriately configured 2-of-3 multisig, not all wallets. Multisig does not automatically solve scams, user error, coercion, or inheritance. Test recovery before trusting a wallet with meaningful funds. Never type seed phrases or passphrases into a website, form, or demo. ← 1 · Terms ← Previous Terms Step 2 of 16 3 · Pick your path → Next → Pick your path
