text: Three keys · Step 4 of 16 Checklist You will need for offline testing: Complete offline tester ZIP · Website tools only ZIP Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → Plebum Dominium teaches self-custody without a hardware wallet. Create and verify keys with offline software, put the backups on metal, and check that they restore the intended wallet. Use offline software to sign. Hardware wallets are optional signing tools introduced only after the metal backups are complete and checked. ← 3 · Pick your path Step 4 of 16 · Checklist 5 · Two boots → Prepare the materials and the recovery plan before creating keys. Private workspace Fair dice with readable faces, a fixed reading order, a numbered recording sheet, and a pen. A workspace without cameras, microphones, or observers recording secrets. Time to stop and investigate any mismatch without rushing. Verified offline setup Prepare the Tails USB and a separate transfer USB. Read Two boots and Check the files before using downloads. Transfer media must never carry signing secrets back online. The kit contains version-pinned instructions. Confirm that each release, signature and hash belong together; do not substitute a newer binary while keeping an old manifest. Compatibility and version reconciliation remain under review. Backup materials Plan durable backups for three independently created signing seeds, one seed per clearly identified backup. Choose locations so one event does not expose or destroy a signing quorum. Choose a backup format you can read and test. Product capacity varies; this guide does not require a particular brand or forbid additional secured copies. Recovery records Preserve a verified public descriptor or compatible wallet-configuration backup containing all three cosigners’ public information, key origins, derivation paths and the 2-of-3 policy. Two seeds alone do not supply the missing cosigner’s public information. Prepare a private location record and instructions a trusted helper can understand. Rehearse with a disposable test wallet before relying on the process for savings. Before proceeding: review how you will recover at least two signing keys and the complete 2-of-3 wallet configuration. Having the equipment is not proof that the wallet is recoverable. ← 3 · Pick your path ← Previous Pick your path Step 4 of 16 5 · Two boots → Next → Two boots

title: Two boots
text: Three keys · Step 5 of 16 Two boots ← 4 · Checklist Step 5 of 16 · Two boots 6 · Check the files → Time 45 min Difficulty Careful Steps 4 sections You will need: Everyday computer · Tails USB You will need for offline testing: Complete offline tester ZIP Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → Separate online preparation from offline secret handling. This page explains the session boundaries. Read Check the files and complete verification before installing or running downloaded software. Page order is not permission to skip that check. Limits: Tails and Offline Mode cannot make compromised hardware or firmware trustworthy. Reusing one computer for several keys creates shared risks that a reboot does not remove. Online preparation Download and verify first Follow the official Tails installation instructions for your computer and release. Authenticate the image before writing it. Keep a separate data USB for the specific verified files you need. Do not put seed phrases, raw entropy, private keys, or passphrases on the data USB or in the everyday operating system. Do not create or unlock Persistent Storage for this guide’s temporary secret-handling sessions. Offline session Set the boundary before secrets At the Tails Welcome Screen, enable Offline Mode before starting the desktop. Older instructions may call this networking disabled. Disconnect network cables and do not enable networking during the session. Use only the verified local tools required for the task. A webpage’s “offline” badge is a reminder, not proof of network isolation or a safe computer. One key or three? The one-key path creates one seed. The three-key path uses a separate session for each seed. Do not load multiple signing seeds in one session. Separate sessions reduce accidental mixing; they do not establish independent hardware trust. Transfer boundary Export only what the next step needs When the guide calls for a transfer, export only reviewed public wallet information or the required transaction file. Public descriptors and xpubs expose wallet activity and still need privacy protection. Never copy seeds, raw entropy, private-key exports, or secret-bearing wallet files back to the online computer. Do not assume a file is public because its name says “backup.” Inspect the export type and follow the wallet’s documentation. End the session Power off fully Finish the offline task and shut down Tails completely before another key session. Do not substitute suspend or hibernate. Keep your physical backup private, away from cameras and microphones. Shutdown ends the session; it does not undo a disclosure, erase a file you saved elsewhere, or remove malicious firmware. If isolation or software integrity is in doubt, stop and investigate before using that key. Stop if: verification is incomplete, networking was enabled while a secret was present, a secret was saved to transfer media, or you cannot identify what an export contains. Do not use a real funded wallet for a rehearsal. Official references: Welcome Screen and Offline Mode · Untrusted computer risks . Next, Check the files. Return to these session rules when the later steps require offline work. ← 4 · Checklist ← Previous Checklist Step 5 of 16 6 · Check the files → Next → Check the files

title: Check the files
text: Three keys · Step 6 of 16 Check the files ← 5 · Two boots Step 6 of 16 · Check the files 7 · Make three keys → Time About 30 min Approach One file at a time Checks Source · signer · contents Verification files at a glance Interactive controls are unavailable. All guided instructions are shown below. The software download: the file whose contents you check. Checksum list: the expected hashes; authenticate this list before relying on it. Signature: verify it over the named file or checksum list using the authenticated key. Publisher’s public key: confirm its full fingerprint independently. It is not your wallet seed or private key. Start with Guided checks , or explore the files and example outcomes. Diagrams and sample hashes explain the process; this page does not verify your downloads. 01 Guided checks One check at a time 02 Understand the files See what connects 03 Stop or continue? Explore the outcomes Check the files Start here Before you run it, know what you downloaded. A download needs more than a familiar logo. Answer three questions about each file before you use it. example-app.zip Start with one file Have these ready: your download, the project’s current verification instructions, and any verification files those instructions require. Choose a checkpoint to see the action, the reason, and what a pass means. 1 The right source? Find the exact project release. 2 The expected signer? Check the key and signature. 3 The same contents? Match your file to the reference. CHECKPOINT 1 / 3 Start at the project. Match your download. Use the project’s official instructions for your version and operating system. Keep that page open while you check. 1 Confirm the project’s domain through a source you already trust. Avoid ads and unsolicited download links. 2 Choose the release and platform you intend to use. 3 Save the download and its required verification files together. What this establishes You have identified the intended release. You still need the publisher and file-content checks. Follow the release, not the logo Project’s official instructions Confirm you have the right source ↓ select exact version + operating system Your download example-app.zip ↓ collect its required companions Verification files A signature, signed list, or project verifier File names here are examples. Each project supplies its own verification process. HTTPS protects the connection. It does not establish software safety. Next: check the signer → CHECKPOINT 2 / 3 Make sure the signature belongs to the right key. Use the publisher’s public verification key . This is separate from your wallet keys: file verification never needs your seed words or private keys. Establish whose key you expect, then check what it signed. 1 Follow the publisher’s documented process to confirm the signing key’s full fingerprint using an independently trusted source. 2 Use the project’s verifier or documented signature commands for the exact release. 3 Confirm the signature covers your download directly, or the checksum list that names your file. What this establishes A valid signature connects the signed content to the authenticated signing key. It does not audit the program’s code. Two checks that belong together Expected publisher’s key Full fingerprint independently confirmed ↓ use this key to verify Signature checks out For the download or its checksum list ↓ now you can use Authenticated signed content Compare the named file if a list was signed “Good signature” + unknown key is incomplete. A new key or unexplained fingerprint change needs investigation. No signature available? Use the publisher’s documented alternative. Do not treat an unsigned hash as publisher proof. Next: check your copy → CHECKPOINT 3 / 3 Compare your file with the expected hash. A SHA-256 hash is a 64-character digest of a file’s contents. Calculate yours and compare all 64 characters with the authenticated reference for that exact file. Windows macOS Linux Get-FileHash -LiteralPath ".\example-app.zip" -Algorithm SHA256 | Format-List PowerShell · run in the file’s folder, or use its full path Copy command What a match means Your file matches the referenced bytes. If the reference itself is unauthenticated, a match alone does not establish who published the file. If the publisher signs the download directly, follow its documented direct-signature process. A separate checksum list may not be required. Illustration only Show a mismatch Authenticated expected hash 9f3a18c7d42e6b508a9174c3e65f20b77dc58a014b2e939f6a70d1c84e5b6230 Calculated hash of your copy 9f3a18c7d42e6b508a9174c3e65f20b77dc58a014b2e939f6a70d1c84e5b6230 All 64 characters match These values are made-up teaching examples, not a checksum for a real download. Keep a record: filename, release, full hash, method, and key fingerprint where applicable. Explore stop / continue → Stop when something is unexplained. A wrong hash, failed signature, unknown key, or uncertain release needs investigation before you run the file. What if a signature checker reports an untrusted key? A valid signature and local key-trust settings answer different questions. “Not certified” may reflect your local trust configuration, but you still need to independently establish the key’s identity. Investigate an unexpected key, bad signature, or unresolved warning. Check the files · explain the pieces File roles Four files. Different jobs. The extra downloads can feel like clutter until you see what each one does. This example follows a project that publishes a signed checksum list. One release folder · select a file below to understand its role A example-app.zip The software you intend to use. B SHA256SUMS The expected hash for each release file. C SHA256SUMS.asc The signature for that checksum list. D publisher-key.asc The public key used to check the signature. This is the download you are checking. Calculate a hash from this file’s contents. Match it to the entry for this exact filename in the authenticated checksum list. What this file does not tell you Its name, icon, and successful download do not prove who published it. How the evidence connects Signed-list example 1 · Establish the reference Authenticated publisher key + Signature + checksum list ↓ Verify the signature over the list Expected hash from an authenticated list Confirm the key fingerprint independently first. 2 · Examine your copy Your downloaded example-app.zip + A SHA-256 calculation tool ↓ Calculate the digest of your copy Calculated hash for the downloaded file Use a trusted tool, following the project’s instructions. AUTHENTICATED EXPECTED HASH ↔ YOUR CALCULATED HASH Same filename. Same release. Every character. A full match links your copy to the authenticated reference. A mismatch means stop and investigate. Some projects sign the download directly. In that case, verify the signature over the downloaded file using the authenticated key. Use the publisher’s actual filenames and instructions; the four filenames above are examples. Check the files · see the outcome Example outcomes Know when to stop. Know what to do next. Explore four sample results. The decision map shows exactly where a verification attempt needs more work. Everything lines up All checks established Only the hash matches Reference not authenticated “Good signature” Signer’s identity unknown One character differs Calculated hash mismatch Example verification path 1 Right source, file, and release? YES · continue ↓ 2 Expected key identity established? YES · continue ↓ 3 Signature over the list valid? YES · continue ↓ 4 Your file’s hash matches its entry? YES · continue ↓ RECORD THE FILE-CHECK RESULT Selected scenario The file checks line up. You identified the release, independently authenticated the publisher key, verified its signature on the checksum list, and matched the entire hash for your file. File checks complete for this example Record what you checked. This establishes the file’s connection to the authenticated release reference. What you do next Keep the filename, release, full hash, method, and key fingerprint in your verification record. Continue only when the guide’s other release and testing requirements are also satisfied. This map illustrates a signed checksum list. A project’s direct-file signature or dedicated verification tool may use a different route. A successful file check does not establish that software is bug-free or approved for custody. Current instructions always come from the project: Tails installation ↗ Sparrow verification ↗ Public test site: the tools and instructions remain under review. Never enter signing secrets into the live website. Successful file checks do not certify software safety or approve a custody release. Testing Plebum Dominium’s own downloads? For public-fixture testing: use the manifest and instructions supplied with your exact package version. You will need for offline testing: Fingerprint checker · ZIP checksums Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → Check your actual files Use the verification tools The diagrams above use examples. These controls open the working checkers for Plebum Dominium’s published files; your selected file stays on your device. 1. Check the downloaded ZIP Open the download verifier, select the complete or focused tester ZIP and compare its result with the exact release you intended to download. Save the verifier separately before going offline; a packaged copy cannot contain its own final ZIP hash. Download ZIP verifier HTML ↓ Open ZIP verifier in a new tab Expected: the filename, byte count and SHA-256 match a listed package. An earlier-version match still refers to that earlier release. 2. Check an individual HTML tool Download the checker, open the saved file in a fresh offline session, choose the intended tool from its menu, then select the downloaded HTML file. The checker calculates its SHA-256 and compares it with the pre-filled reference for the dice converter, Diceware mapper or wallet-map tool. Download fingerprint checker HTML ↓ Open fingerprint checker in a new tab Expected: an exact match to the intended tool. Stop on a mismatch or an unrecognized digest. A matching hash confirms agreement with the listed reference. It does not replace the source, signer or software-review checks above. After extraction, run the package’s verify_package.py to check all included files. A package checksum checks consistency with its reference; it does not independently audit code or establish publisher identity. Review and authenticate any verification script before running it. Keep a verification record: release, exact filename, full hash, method, and signing-key fingerprint when applicable. Verify every required file before beginning your path’s offline secret-handling session. ← 5 · Two boots ← Previous Two boots Step 6 of 16 7 · Make three keys → Next → Make three keys

title: Make three keys
text: Three keys · Step 7 of 16 Make the three keys ← 6 · Check the files Step 7 of 16 · Make three keys 8 · Build the 2-of-3 → Time 30-45 min Difficulty Moderate Steps 6 sections You will need: 5 dice · Paper and pen · The worksheet You will need for offline testing: Dice converter HTML · Python dice converter Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → Learn how dice rolls become three separate 24-word seed phrases. During this public review, follow the method with the supplied public test rolls and mnemonic fixtures. Label every record TEST ONLY; these tools and instructions remain under review. These are learning records for the disposable rehearsal ahead. Never use public fixtures or practice keys for real funds. Read Build the 2-of-3 to understand the structure, then choose the practice network and create the separate test wallet on Set up a test wallet . Safety first: Never enter seed words on an online computer. Boot Tails with networking Disabled before you start. Shut down fully between each key. What you will do Boot Tails offline. Copy the dice converter page. Roll dice. Enter the faces. The page counts to 256 bits. Write down the 24 words. Prove them with a second tool. Repeat for Seed 2 and Seed 3, with a full shutdown between each. Step 1 / 6 Boot Tails. Copy the converter. Boot Tails with networking set to Disabled. Copy the checked dice converter page from the data USB to the Desktop. Check: Open the checked local copy after disabling networking in Tails. Confirm the operating system’s network status. Tor Browser may still report an online flag; that flag alone proves neither connection nor isolation. If you cannot establish the OS network state, stop. Use the tool · Step 1 Open the dice converter alongside this guide The converter accepts your recorded faces and displays the 256-bit input and 24 BIP39 words. It does not roll the dice for you. Download dice converter HTML ↓ Open dice converter in a new tab Use the saved file: download and check it before disconnecting. Disable networking in the operating system, then open the saved HTML file and complete its two public-test confirmations. The website copy stays locked. A browser connection flag does not establish network isolation. Use public-tests/T5-dice-reference-inputs.txt and the public-tests/fixtures/ files from your verified complete or tools-only package for this rehearsal. Keep every record marked TEST ONLY . Enter the example faces in the converter. Continue to Step 2 below to check accepted pairs and the bit count. Compare the complete result using Step 4. Return to this guide tab when you finish, then use Lock and clear in the tool before changing network settings. Public dice example and expected result · Check the tool’s fingerprint Use the exact package and fingerprints listed on Downloads . The November 13 candidate changes dice-validation behavior and needs its own affected checks. Earlier R3 results apply only to that recorded package and scope. Use public fixtures and disposable test passwords only; real-wallet use remains outside this release. Step 2 / 6 Roll the dice. Enter the faces. Roll five dice at once. Enter each face as you roll it. Using fair, independently rolled dice and a fixed reading order, faces 1 to 4 count as bits (1=00, 2=01, 3=10, 4=11). Faces 5 and 6 are skipped, roll those dice again. The page counts the pairs and stops you at 128. SHAKE 1 SHAKE 2 SHAKE 3 11 RE-ROLL 01 00 10 01 01 RE-ROLL 11 11 00 10 00 10 RE-ROLL 00 01 RE-ROLL 10 256-BIT STRING 11 00 10 01 01 01 11 00 10 11 00 10 00 01 10 …keep rolling… 256 / 256 BITS 10 / 256 20 / 256 30 / 256 256 / 256 24 WORDS Roll as many times as needed to get 256 bits of entropy: about 39 shakes. Check: The page shows 128 pairs and 256 bits. Count accepted pairs, not an estimated number of shakes. Step 3 / 6 Write the 24 words. At 256 bits the page prints 24 words. In a 24-word BIP39 phrase, the last word contains three entropy bits and eight checksum bits. It is not an arbitrary check word: never invent or alter it. Write all 24 on the grid. Compare them privately in order, away from cameras and microphones. Check: All 24 words and their positions are recorded accurately; a valid checksum does not prove safe randomness. Step 4 / 6 Prove it with a second tool. Use a separately verified offline implementation with the exact same 256-bit entropy and BIP39 settings. Raw dice inputs are not interchangeable between tools: some hash the roll string while this guide maps accepted faces to bit pairs. Confirm the input method before comparing all 24 words. If you cannot establish that the inputs and method match, stop; do not guess or choose a preferred output. Check: Both tools show the same 24 words. Step 5 / 6 Shut down. Start the next key. Shut Tails down fully. Wait until the screen is dark. Then boot again for Seed 2. New rolls, new words. Repeat for Seed 3. Never continue a list from the previous boot. Check: Each seed has its own 24 words on its own grid. Three grids total. Step 6 / 6 Confirm the checks agree. The checksum detects many transcription errors, but not all of them. It does not authenticate the source of the words. At least two checks must agree: the two tools showing the same words, and the wallet (Sparrow or Electrum, offline) opening the list without error. If anything disagrees, stop. Stop if: The operating system is connected or its network state is uncertain, the two tools show different words, or the wallet rejects the list. Lock and clear the tool, then investigate before restarting the rehearsal. Next, Build the 2-of-3. ← 6 · Check the files ← Previous Check the files Step 7 of 16 8 · Build the 2-of-3 → Next → Build the 2-of-3

title: Build the 2-of-3
text: Three keys · Step 8 of 16 Build the 2-of-3 Plebum Dominium teaches self-custody without a hardware wallet. Create and verify keys with offline software, put the backups on metal, and check that they restore the intended wallet. Use offline software to sign. Hardware wallets are optional signing tools introduced only after the metal backups are complete and checked. ← 7 · Make three keys Step 8 of 16 · Build the 2-of-3 9 · Set up a test wallet → Time 45-60 min Difficulty Careful Steps 7 steps You will need for the walkthrough: Public practice records · Verified Sparrow You will need for offline testing: 2-of-3 demo Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → A 2-of-3 watch-only wallet is built from three public keys. One seed per offline boot supplies each public key. The exported wallet map can reconstruct the wallet’s addresses and watch its transactions; it cannot sign by itself. Read the structure first. The seven steps below explain the process. Before doing the hands-on rehearsal, continue to Set up a test wallet to select the test network, create disposable keys, and save temporary recovery records. Use that network’s verified settings for practice. This public review uses no real wallet secrets or funds. Safety first: Never enter seed words on an online computer. You will boot Tails four times: once per seed to copy its public key, then once more with no seed to build the vault. Recorded walkthrough versions: Sparrow 2.5.5, Tails 7.16 and Electrum 4.8.3. Check current publisher releases and version-specific verification before a new test. Record the actual versions you use; the earlier results do not establish compatibility for a newer release. How the build works Boot Tails offline. Launch Sparrow from the terminal. Extract each seed's public key, one per boot. Build the 2-of-3 vault with no seed. Export the map. Independently verify the cosigners and wallet policy, then compare several receiving addresses. Step 1 / 7 Boot Tails. Networking stays off. The entire sheet happens with networking Disabled. Check it on every boot. Step 2 / 7 Open the terminal. Launch Sparrow. The commands below use the recorded Sparrow 2.5.5 filename. For another verified release, substitute its exact archive filename. Run these commands one at a time. Wait for each command to finish before entering the next. The shell prompt is not part of a command. cd ~/Desktop tar -xvf sparrowwallet-2.5.5-x86_64.tar.gz cd Sparrow ./bin/Sparrow Sparrow may take 15 to 30 seconds to open. The terminal may remain occupied while Sparrow runs. If a command reports an error or the expected window does not open, stop and investigate; text color alone is not an error check. Step 3 / 7 New wallet: 2 of 3, native Segwit. File → New Wallet. Pick Multi Signature, Native Segwit, 2 of 3. Confirm the selected network and the documented derivation settings for every signer before exporting public keys. Mainnet reference: m/48'/0'/0'/2' is the example path for the intended mainnet setup described here. It is not an instruction to force the practice wallet onto mainnet settings. For the disposable rehearsal, use the selected test network’s documented settings. Do not reuse its keys for the eventual mainnet wallet. Check: Network, 2-of-3 policy, script type, and derivation settings agree with independently verified signer records. Stop if any setting is unexplained. Step 4 / 7 Keystore 1: Seed 1 in, public key out. Keystore 1 → New or Imported Software Wallet → type Seed 1's 24 words. Export the xpub. Save it to the data USB as s1-xpub.txt . Close Sparrow. Shut down. Wait for a dark screen. Step 5 / 7 Twice more. One seed per boot. Boot again for Seed 2 → s2-xpub.txt . Shut down. Boot again for Seed 3 → s3-xpub.txt . Shut down. Check: Three xpub files on the USB. One seed per boot, never two. Step 6 / 7 Fresh boot. No seed. Build the vault. Boot Tails again. Do not type any seed. New wallet → Multi Signature → Native Segwit → 2 of 3 → import the three xpub files. Confirm the path. Export the output descriptor to the data USB. That file is the wallet map. Try the 2-of-3 demo → Why keep the descriptor and all three seed backups? Lost a seed plate? Two seeds + the wallet map. The verified descriptor supplies the missing signer’s public key. The two surviving keys can sign. Lost the wallet map? All three seeds + the original setup. The third seed supplies the missing public key, so you can rebuild the descriptor without the saved file. Spending still takes two signatures. Step 7 / 7 · Before funding Verify the wallet independently Matching addresses alone cannot prove a coordinator is honest if both devices use the same unverified descriptor. 01 · Record addresses Record several complete receiving addresses from Sparrow offline. Write the full strings, not just QR codes. 02 · Verify each cosigner On a separate trusted offline device, compare each cosigner’s master fingerprint, derivation path, and extended public key with records obtained directly from that signing session, not solely from the coordinator. 03 · Check the wallet policy Confirm the 2-of-3 threshold, native SegWit script type, and full descriptor including key order and checksum where supported. 04 · Rebuild and compare Reconstruct a watch-only wallet from independently verified details. Compare several receiving addresses character for character. Never enter seeds on a networked device. Stop before funding if anything differs. If a key, fingerprint, path, policy, or address differs, investigate offline. Two devices using the same substituted descriptor may show matching attacker-controlled addresses. Next, Set up a test wallet . Complete that preparation before practicing spending and recovery. ← 7 · Make three keys ← Previous Make three keys Step 8 of 16 9 · Set up a test wallet → Next → Set up a test wallet

title: Set up a test wallet
text: Three keys · Step 9 of 16 Set up a test wallet ← 8 · Build the 2-of-3 Step 9 of 16 · Set up a test wallet 10 · Practice spending and recovery → Test wallet only. Never reuse these test seeds, passphrases or dice rolls for your real wallet. Generate fresh, independent secrets after the rehearsal. Offline signing computer: create test keys, restore and sign with OS networking disabled. Online watch-only computer: receive, prepare transactions and broadcast; never import signing secrets. These labels are reminders, not a network-isolation test. Prepare a separate practice wallet before spending and recovery exercises. 1. Select the test network Sparrow documents Tools → Restart in Testnet . Confirm the network shown by your installed version, and use a server, faucet and explorer for that same network. Different test networks are not interchangeable. Test coins are for practice. Do not send real bitcoin, pay for test coins, or give a faucet seed words or a passphrase. A faucet needs only the intended public receive address. Interfaces and services can differ from mainnet. 2. Build a separate practice wallet Create three new disposable keys and a test-only 2-of-3 wallet using the structure explained in Build the 2-of-3 . Label the wallet and every record TEST ONLY . Keep all signing secrets in the offline signing environment; the online coordinator stays watch-only. Verify the threshold, script type, all three cosigner public keys and their origins against independent signer records. A matching receive address alone does not prove the coordinator is trustworthy. These practice keys must never hold real funds. 3. Save temporary recovery records Keep a separate temporary seed record for each practice key. Save the complete wallet configuration containing all three cosigners’ public information, key origins, derivation paths and the 2-of-3 policy. Record the selected network and the wallet details needed to recognize the intended wallet. Check that the records are readable and correspond to the practice wallet. Keep them until the spending and recovery exercises are finished. Use these disposable paper records for the spending and recovery rehearsal. Metal work is outside T7 and comes later in the guide. Hardware signers are optional and come only after durable metal backups are complete and checked. 4. Check you are ready to practice Before receiving test coins, confirm that the wallet, signers and services use the same test network and that the temporary recovery records are complete. Verify the intended receive address using the signer’s documented checks and independent wallet records. Next, continue to Practice spending and recovery with your checked temporary records. The later metal-backup stage is outside this rehearsal. That sheet covers the transaction and the restore exercise together. Keep the disposable wallet separate from any intended mainnet setup. Pause and check: Stop if the network is unclear, a real wallet’s signing secrets are involved, or any temporary seed record or configuration is missing. Never promote a practice seed into a mainnet backup. ← 8 · Build the 2-of-3 ← Previous Build the 2-of-3 Step 9 of 16 10 · Practice spending and recovery → Next → Practice spending and recovery

title: Practice spending and recovery
text: Three keys · Step 10 of 16 Practice spending and recovery Use verified Sparrow software in offline Tails for signing. Here, a signer means a distinct key used in an offline session, not a required hardware wallet. Check the disposable paper seed records and complete test wallet map before starting. Metal work is outside T7; finish this software rehearsal before the later metal-backup stage. Optional hardware signing must wait for checked metal backups. ← 9 · Set up a test wallet Step 10 of 16 · Practice spending and recovery 11 · Back up your keys and wallet map → Test wallet only. Never reuse these test seeds, passphrases or dice rolls for your real wallet. Generate fresh, independent secrets after the rehearsal. Offline signing computer: create test keys, restore and sign with OS networking disabled. Online watch-only computer: receive, prepare transactions and broadcast; never import signing secrets. These labels are reminders, not a network-isolation test. Use the disposable test wallet to practice a transaction, then check recovery from its temporary records. Continue with your disposable test wallet Use the wallet prepared in the previous sheet, Set up a test wallet . Check its test network, three disposable keys, temporary seed records and complete 2-of-3 configuration. Never use a real wallet’s seeds for this exercise. Receive test coins at the independently checked practice-wallet address and wait for confirmation on the selected test network. Keep the online coordinator watch-only. Each signer needs the correct wallet policy and relevant key information; restoring a seed alone does not establish the intended multisig wallet. For each offline signing wallet, import one test seed as a software key and the other two keys as public information. Verify the complete 2-of-3 policy before opening the PSBT. Do not persist a wallet containing secrets. 1. Build and inspect Online watch-only computer In the online watch-only wallet, choose the destination, amount and fee, then export the unsigned PSBT. Record the intended payment using destination information obtained independently from the recipient, not just copied from the coordinator display. A PSBT carries transaction and signing information. It is not a seed backup and can expose financial metadata. Transfer only the intended transaction file, never a wallet containing private keys. 2. Verify before the first signature Offline signing computer: first key In the first offline software signing session, check the network, wallet policy, full recipient address, amount and total fee. Account for every output: any change must return to the verified wallet. Stop if the signer cannot identify change or explain an output. Use Sparrow’s transaction review in the offline session. Paper notes help compare intent but do not make a compromised computer trustworthy. For the Tails software-signing workflow, start in Offline Mode and load only this signer’s secret. Export the partially signed PSBT, then fully shut down. 3. Review again with the second key Offline signing computer: second key Use a different key belonging to the same verified 2-of-3 wallet. Review the same transaction independently, including all outputs and the fee, before signing. A file name or signature count alone is not verification. For software signing, use a fresh offline session. Rebooting the same computer does not provide independent hardware or remove a firmware compromise. Do not collect both seeds in the online coordinator or one saved wallet file. 4. Finalize and broadcast Return the signed PSBT to the online coordinator, finalize it when the required signatures are present for every input, and review the resulting transaction before broadcasting. Watch for confirmation on the selected network. If any field changes unexpectedly, stop and investigate. Do not sign a replacement you have not reviewed. A confirmation shows that this transaction was accepted; it does not establish that the backups or other signer pairs work. 5. Recover from the temporary backups Reconstruct the disposable wallet from its saved configuration and temporary seed records in a separate test environment, keeping the original practice wallet and records available for comparison. Do not wipe a real working wallet. Check the recovered policy, all three cosigners’ public information, known receive addresses and transaction history against the independent practice records. Then rehearse spending with each intended pair of distinct signers. An address match alone does not complete the recovery exercise. Work from copies and keep the original test records intact. Simulate a missing seed record by withholding one copy: the two surviving keys plus the complete saved configuration should recover the practice wallet. Then simulate a missing wallet-map copy: use all three test seed backups and the recorded original setup to reconstruct the public configuration. Compare the recovered policy and addresses, then test the intended signer pairs. Do not destroy records to simulate loss. Record which recovery paths and signer pairs worked, and resolve discrepancies before relying on the process. 6. Finish the rehearsal Keep the practice wallet and records clearly separated while learning, including the backup and wallet-map exercises on the following sheets. Retire them only after the whole rehearsal is finished. Never reuse its seeds for real funds. The next sheet, Back up your keys and wallet map , explains durable records and storage. Any later mainnet setup needs fresh keys, its own verified configuration and its own recovery checks. A successful rehearsal does not verify that later wallet or certify these public-test tools for real secrets. Pause and check: Stop if the wallet policy is uncertain, an output is unexplained, a fee is unexpected, or a signing secret reaches an online environment. ← 9 · Set up a test wallet ← Previous Set up a test wallet Step 10 of 16 11 · Back up your keys and wallet map → Next → Back up your keys and wallet map

title: Back up your keys and wallet map
text: Three keys · Step 11 of 16 Back up your keys and wallet map Complete and check the metal backups before introducing any optional hardware wallet. Software signing and recovery remain the default. T6 and T7 use disposable paper records; metal work is outside those tests. Read this later-stage guidance after the software rehearsal. Never photograph or record engraved secrets. ← 10 · Practice spending and recovery Step 11 of 16 · Back up your keys and wallet map 12 · Protect the wallet map → Plan durable seed backups and preserve the complete wallet configuration. After the spending and recovery rehearsal: your practice wallet remains TEST ONLY. T7 ends with disposable paper records; metal work is outside the test. Read this later-stage guidance using fictional records. A future intended wallet needs fresh keys, its own verified configuration, and checks of its actual backups before funding; a successful test-wallet recovery does not verify those records. The tools remain under public review. Record accurately Back up each of the three seeds separately on metal using the plate maker’s recording instructions. Preserve word order and any required encoding information. Work privately and compare every entry against the original. Keep the original protected while checking the replacement. A damaged or ambiguous mark needs correction before you rely on it. Check recovery safely Read the metal record back, then restore it with verified offline software in a fresh Tails session. For multisig, load only one seed per boot and use the complete public configuration. Compare the recorded wallet settings and several full addresses, then rehearse signing on the designated test network. Do not wipe your only working signer to test an unproven backup. Never type seeds into this website or an online form. For a rehearsal, use a disposable test wallet. For an existing funded wallet, plan the verification carefully before changing devices or backups. Keep the complete recovery information Preserve a verified public descriptor or compatible wallet-configuration backup containing all three cosigners’ public information, key origins, derivation paths and the 2-of-3 policy. Two seeds alone do not supply the missing cosigner’s public information. Lost a seed plate? Two seeds + the wallet map. The verified descriptor supplies the missing signer’s public key. The two surviving keys can sign. Lost the wallet map? All three seeds + the original setup. The third seed supplies the missing public key, so you can rebuild the descriptor without the saved file. Spending still takes two signatures. The spending and recovery exercise covers both scenarios with disposable records. Preserve the originals while working from test copies. Try the 2-of-3 demo → A public-only descriptor cannot sign by itself, but it reveals wallet information. Confirm that the export contains no private keys before treating it as public data. Protect its availability and privacy. Plan copies and locations Balance loss, theft, access, and disaster risks. More copies can improve availability and also expose secrets in more places. Document which locations contain which material; do not combine enough signing secrets in one place to defeat your separation plan. Do not destroy an original merely because a new backup looks correct. Retire it only after a successful recovery check and a deliberate review of the remaining copies. Revisit the plan when locations or helpers change. Stop if: a backup is unreadable, the recovered wallet differs, or any required passphrase or configuration is missing. Do not overwrite or discard the remaining working material. ← 10 · Practice spending and recovery ← Previous Practice spending and recovery Step 11 of 16 12 · Protect the wallet map → Next → Protect the wallet map

title: Protect the wallet map
text: Three keys · Step 12 of 16 Protect the wallet map You will need for offline testing: Wallet-map tool HTML · Python wallet-map tool Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → ← 11 · Back up your keys and wallet map Step 12 of 16 · Protect the wallet map 13 · If I am gone → Protect the wallet map’s privacy without making recovery depend on an untested file. Understand the map A verified public-only descriptor describes the wallet’s scripts, cosigner public keys and derivation information. It can reveal wallet activity but cannot sign by itself. Some exports contain private keys: confirm the export type before treating it as public data. Keep the complete verified configuration. Do not assume three seeds alone automatically recover every script type, derivation path or wallet setting. Encryption protects confidentiality; it does not replace configuration backups. Choose a recoverable protection plan Decide who needs access after loss or incapacity. Keep more than one protected copy, with a durable record of the decryption method and its password or required key. Avoid making every copy depend on one forgotten password. The file-encryption password is separate from a Bitcoin wallet passphrase and a device PIN. Do not reuse signing secrets as encryption passwords. Arrange separate access to encrypted copies and their unlocking material without making either impossible for your recovery plan. Use the HTML wallet-map tool For this rehearsal, encrypt and restore the supplied public sample text. The tool protects a saved map’s contents; it does not create or validate a wallet descriptor. Download wallet-map tool HTML ↓ Open wallet-map tool in a new tab Use the saved file: download and check it before disconnecting. Disable networking in the operating system, then open the saved HTML file and complete its two public-test confirmations. The website copy stays locked. A browser connection flag does not establish network isolation. Open public-tests/fixtures/public-map.txt from your verified complete or tools-only package. Use a disposable test password. Encrypt the sample and save the result. Decrypt the saved file and compare the entire recovered text with the original. Check the wrong-password and damaged-file cases in the wallet-map retest instructions . Keep the original sample for comparison. Use Lock and clear when finished, then return to this guide tab for the recovery checks below. Use the exact package and fingerprints listed on Downloads . The November 13 candidate changes dice-validation behavior and needs its own affected checks. Earlier R3 results apply only to that recorded package and scope. Use public fixtures and disposable test passwords only; real-wallet use remains outside this release. Verify before replacing any copy Start with harmless sample text. Test decryption in a later session, using the exact software intended for recovery. For a real map, verify the entire recovered contents against the original before relying on the encrypted copy. Keep the existing protected backup until these checks pass. Deleting a file or emptying the trash does not prove every copy has been erased. Plan plaintext handling before writing sensitive material to persistent storage. Keep an independent recovery check Windows and physical Tails results are recorded for the exercised r4 cases. Earlier cross-tool results and automated HTML/Python compatibility checks are also recorded, with their original scope. These results do not establish that every recovery scenario has passed. Use the Python wallet-map tool when following the documented cross-tool test. Tails also includes Kleopatra for its documented file-encryption workflow; follow the official Tails instructions for that separate method. Do not assume different formats are interchangeable. Keep a verified recovery option and the original comparison file. T6/T7 rehearse with disposable paper records; metal comes after testing. Final release and printable-material review remain separate. Pause and check: Stop if decryption fails, the recovered map differs, the export contains unexpected private material, or you cannot explain how a trusted helper would regain access. ← 11 · Back up your keys and wallet map ← Previous Back up your keys and wallet map Step 12 of 16 13 · If I am gone → Next → If I am gone

title: If I am gone
text: Three keys · Step 13 of 16 If I am gone ← 12 · Protect the wallet map Step 13 of 16 · If I am gone 14 · If you get stuck → Help a trusted person find the required records and know when to stop. Leave a clear private plan Describe the wallet type, the location of the full instructions, the required recovery items, and a trusted contact who can explain the process. Keep signing secrets out of this website, email, and the general instruction sheet. Separate ownership and access arrangements from the technical recovery instructions. Make sure the intended person can find the plan when needed. Identify the required items This path requires at least two signing keys and the complete 2-of-3 wallet configuration. Preserve a verified public descriptor or compatible wallet-configuration backup containing all three cosigners’ public information, key origins, derivation paths and the 2-of-3 policy. Two seeds alone do not supply the missing cosigner’s public information. Recover with verified offline software in Tails. Load one signing seed in a fresh offline boot, together with the complete public wallet configuration. Export only the partially signed transaction, then shut down fully before loading a second distinct seed in another offline boot. A fresh boot reduces accidental mixing; it does not remove compromised hardware or firmware. No hardware wallet purchase is required. Confirm the recovered wallet Follow the recorded, rehearsed procedure and verify the policy and wallet details against independent trusted records. An address match alone does not establish that a coordinator is trustworthy. If the wallet is empty or differs from the records, stop. Check the passphrase, account, network, derivation information and synchronization before concluding funds are lost. Do not overwrite backups or create replacement keys as a guess. Practice before an emergency Walk through locating the records and explaining the steps with the intended helper. Use a disposable test wallet for hands-on training, without exposing the owner’s signing secrets. When a legitimate recovery is needed, independently verify the destination and transaction details on trusted signing equipment. A small successful transfer is useful evidence, but it is not a complete audit of the recovery setup. Protect the secrets: no legitimate support agent needs a seed phrase or private key. If the instructions, equipment compatibility, or wallet identity are uncertain, stop before entering secrets or signing. ← 12 · Protect the wallet map ← Previous Protect the wallet map Step 13 of 16 14 · If you get stuck → Next → If you get stuck

title: If you get stuck
text: Three keys · Step 14 of 16 If you get stuck ← 13 · If I am gone Step 14 of 16 · If you get stuck 15 · Tough questions → Find the problem, preserve what still works, and stop when the next step is uncertain. What setup is this? A 2-of-3 wallet uses three distinct signing keys; any two can authorize a spend under the correct wallet policy. What recovery information matters? Keep the complete wallet configuration and all three cosigner public records as well as the signing backups. Losing two signing keys can prevent spending; losing configuration is a separate recovery problem. Three seeds do not guarantee automatic reconstruction. The download or version does not match Stop before running it. Confirm the exact release, file, signature and full hash from the intended publisher. Do not assume a newer release is compatible or an older release is safe. The staging download inventory has unresolved mismatches; see Downloads . The two converters disagree Preserve the original rolls privately. Check transcription, input method, bit order and settings. Do not guess a replacement word or choose whichever output you prefer. Use public test vectors before trusting the procedure; funded-wallet backups must not be edited to make a check pass. The restored wallet looks empty Stop before wiping or discarding anything. Check the network, account, script type, derivation settings, passphrase if used, and synchronization. Preserve working devices and backups while investigating. Never send secrets to someone offering recovery help. Where should secrets be kept? Keep signing secrets offline and protected from theft and loss. Avoid photographs, email, cloud notes and online forms. Plan durable copies and separate locations, then test recovery. A location card is not a substitute for the backups. How can a helper prepare? Practice with a disposable wallet and a private written plan. Use the recovery planning guide where it matches your wallet. Never paste real seeds, passwords or passphrases into this site. ← 13 · If I am gone ← Previous If I am gone Step 14 of 16 15 · Tough questions → Next → Tough questions

title: Tough questions
text: Three keys · Step 15 of 16 Tough questions ← 14 · If you get stuck Step 15 of 16 · Tough questions 16 · Recovery card → Understand what the design protects—and what still depends on your equipment and recovery plan. Does a fresh boot remove every risk? No. Offline sessions reduce network exposure but do not establish trustworthy hardware or firmware. A persistent compromise can observe keys across different boots on the same computer. One key per boot is not independent hardware isolation. Are dice automatically trustworthy? The input must be unpredictable and the conversion correct. Biased rolls, transcription errors or incompatible input methods undermine the result. Observable dice do not eliminate trust in the software that turns rolls into keys. Can one stolen key spend? One distinct key cannot satisfy a correctly configured 2-of-3 policy alone. Two compromised signing keys can. Devices containing copies of the same key do not create independent cosigners. Can I recreate the map from seeds? Do not rely on that as the backup plan. Preserve verified configuration, including script type, key origins and all cosigner public information. Protect its privacy and test that it restores the intended wallet. Should every cosigner have a passphrase? A cosigner passphrase adds a recovery dependency. This guide’s basic three-key route does not require one. Adding any requires documenting exactly which signer uses it and testing the resulting configuration; it is not a substitute for key separation. What proves the plan works? Rehearse setup, signing and recovery with disposable test keys, including the intended signer pairs. A matching receive address or a single successful payment is useful evidence, not proof that a coordinator is trustworthy or every backup works. ← 14 · If you get stuck ← Previous If you get stuck Step 15 of 16 16 · Recovery card → Next → Recovery card

title: Recovery card
text: Three keys · Step 16 of 16 Recovery card The recovery plan must work with offline software and the checked metal backups. A hardware wallet is optional; a device brand or purchase must not be a recovery requirement. ← 15 · Tough questions Step 16 of 16 · Recovery card Review this path → A private pointer to your recovery plan. It does not replace a wallet backup. What this card is for A short location record helps an authorized person find the complete instructions and required materials. It cannot replace at least two signing keys and the complete 2-of-3 wallet configuration. Location information can help a thief too. Protect the card even though it contains no signing secrets. Write these pointers offline Wallet type: 2-of-3 multisig. Where to find the complete recovery instructions. Separate seed-backup locations and wallet-configuration location. Trusted contact and date last reviewed. Location of any separate decryption instructions, if required. Write privately on paper. This page intentionally provides no form for entering real locations or secrets. Never include these No seed words, raw entropy, private keys, wallet passphrases, or decryption passwords on the card. Keep it separate from the materials it points to. A descriptor can contain private keys; only a verified public-only export belongs in the non-signing configuration records. Keep it current Check that the intended person can follow the pointers. Update the record after moving a backup or changing the recovery plan, then account for obsolete copies. The downloadable legacy card/PDF has not yet been reconciled with these revised instructions. Do not treat that older packet as a verified version of this page. Recovery still requires verification: use the complete, rehearsed procedure. A list of locations, a device brand, or a derivation-path label is not sufficient by itself. ← 15 · Tough questions ← Previous Tough questions Step 16 of 16 Review this path → Next → Review this path

title: Chainalysis restores key services after credential exposure
text: Latest development Chainalysis restores key services after credential exposure Updated November 10, 2026 Chainalysis said on November 10 that Data Solutions was back online and customers were being brought back with emailed instructions. It had said on November 7 that Reactor, KYT and Address Screening were back online with additional security measures. The restoration follows a broader disclosure on November 4: names, usernames, password hashes and active access tokens for all users had been exposed. A separate attack also exposed some customer passwords. The company took products offline and notified customers whose KYT accounts appeared to have been accessed without permission. Its recovery instructions call for password resets and API-key rotation where applicable. In its November 4 update, Chainalysis said it had found no evidence that investigation data had been accessed or its address-attribution data altered. That is a statement about the evidence available at that time. Why it matters here Security providers can be breached too. Use a different password for each service, open the known website yourself when checking a security notice, and keep wallet recovery words out of support messages and online accounts. Restored service does not undo information already exposed. Source: Chainalysis incident updates, November 4–10

title: Binance confirms $6.34 billion theft and publishes initial findings
text: Exchange security Binance confirms $6.34 billion theft and publishes initial findings Incident October 29 · Report November 3, 2026 Binance has confirmed the October 29 theft. In its November 3 preliminary report, the exchange put the affected assets at about $6.34 billion and said about $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted. It said it had reserved enough company funds to cover the loss and replenished 98% of the affected token assets. Those figures are Binance’s report for that date; frozen assets are not the same as funds returned. Binance said attackers gained unauthorized access to an internal wallet-signing service. Its account describes compromised employee devices, malicious downloads and fake recruitment interviews. The company said it rebuilt affected systems and was commissioning independent security reviews. Its findings remain preliminary. Why it matters here The practical lesson is to protect the whole signing process: the software you download, the computer you use and the details you approve. A promise to cover an exchange loss still depends on that company. Self-custody transfers responsibility to you, so practice setup, signing and recovery before relying on a wallet. Source: Binance preliminary findings, November 3

title: Mercado Bitcoin theft: investigators estimate $49 million stolen
text: Exchange security Mercado Bitcoin theft: investigators estimate $49 million stolen November 2, 2026 Chainalysis, which helped respond to the November 2 attack on Brazil’s Mercado Bitcoin exchange, estimated that about $49 million was stolen across 17 blockchains. It said its work with law enforcement and asset issuers helped freeze nearly $10 million. The company was still tracing the remaining funds when it published its report. Why it matters here Tracing stolen coins can help an investigation, but it does not guarantee their return. Some centrally issued tokens can be frozen by their issuers; Bitcoin has no equivalent issuer-operated freeze. Verify the receiving address and transaction details before signing. Recovery after a theft is uncertain. Source: Chainalysis incident response report, November 2

title: Coinbase vendor breach exposes customer contact data
text: Data & privacy Coinbase vendor breach exposes customer contact data October 2026 On October 27, 2026, Coinbase said a security incident at Amplitude, a third-party analytics vendor, exposed contact and limited transaction data for a small subset of its customers. Coinbase said its own systems were not breached and customer funds were not affected. The company did not say how many customers were affected or which fields were taken. A claim on X that more than 70,000 users were affected was called false by Coinbase. The company is notifying affected customers and regulators. Why it matters here An exchange can keep your coins safe and still leak your contact details through a vendor you never chose. That data is what makes phishing convincing: a message that knows your name, your phone number, and your recent transactions. Treat any message claiming to be from an exchange as suspect until you verify it through a channel you opened yourself. Keep your seed material entirely off any system tied to an exchange account. Sources: Unchained · CoinDesk · Cointelegraph

title: Keystone breach exposes customer shipping addresses
text: Personal security Keystone breach exposes customer shipping addresses October 2026 On October 24, 2026, Keystone disclosed a website breach that exposed customer shipping data, including home addresses tied to past hardware wallet orders. The company said private keys and funds on its devices were not affected, since that material never touches the internet. Keystone has not said how many customers were affected or how the breach happened. Why it matters here A shipping address tied to a hardware wallet order tells a thief where a holder lives, which enables physical targeting and phishing that references your real order. This guide does not require a hardware wallet. If you choose optional hardware signing after checking your metal backups, review the seller and delivery privacy, and treat unexpected messages about the order as suspect. Sources: AltcoinDaily

title: State Bank of India: 3,897 customer records on the dark web
text: Data & privacy State Bank of India: 3,897 customer records on the dark web October 2026 On October 21, 2026, State Bank of India disclosed an incident involving customer data on the dark web. The bank said it was alerted on October 16 by its threat intelligence provider, the Defence Cyber Agency, and CERT-In. A preliminary analysis of about 375,000 records found 3,897 customer records containing personal information. Those records included names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and customer identifiers, and loan and lead metadata. The bank said customer balances were completely safe, that the incident had no material impact on core operations, and that it had engaged an independent CERT-In empanelled agency for a full assessment. Why it matters here A bank can keep balances safe and still leak your home address, your phone number, and your loan history. That is the data used for targeted phishing and for physical targeting. Treat any message claiming to be from a bank or an exchange as suspect until you verify it through a separate channel you trust, and keep your plates, your map, and your passphrase paper in separate places, away from anything tied to that leaked identity data. Sources: Reuters · The Hindu BusinessLine

title: South Korea: hacking incidents at seven banks linked to one attacker
text: Institutional security South Korea: hacking incidents at seven banks linked to one attacker October 2026 On October 4, 2026, South Korean financial authorities said hacking incidents at seven financial institutions appeared to be linked to the same attacker. The institutions named were Shinhan, KB Kookmin, Hana, BNK Busan Bank, Yeogaram, Welcome Savings Bank, and Hyundai Capital. Authorities shared the attacker's internet addresses and security precautions with about 500 firms in the sector and started urgent inspections. At Shinhan, information leaked through a system used by employees and loan recruiters. Customer internet and mobile banking were not affected, and no financial losses were reported there. Authorities grouped the incidents into information inquiry services, employee support services, and website services. Why it matters here The entry point was not the main customer banking system. It was employee and recruiter systems around it. That is a reason not to trust a large institution to protect every piece of your identity data, and a reason to keep seed material out of any system tied to a bank, a loan application, or an employer portal. Your plates and your map do not belong in the same place as your banking identity. Sources: Aju Press · Tech Insider

title: Two hardware failures in one year
text: Hardware & keys Two hardware failures in one year October 2026 In July 2026, attackers drained about 1,816 bitcoin from more than 5,200 Coldcard wallets. The cause was a firmware flaw from March 2021 that left some seeds with as little as 40 bits of real randomness instead of 128. Updating the firmware did not fix seeds already made. Owners had to move their funds to new seeds. In October 2026, Ledger confirmed an unauthorized hardware implant in at least one device sold by the Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis. Researchers estimate $86 million to $93 million was taken from hundreds of wallets. Ledger said its own systems and direct sales were not affected, and every confirmed case so far traces to that reseller. Why it matters here Plebum Dominium teaches self-custody without a hardware wallet. Create and verify keys with offline software, record them on metal, and test recovery. Hardware wallets are optional signing tools only after those backups are complete and checked. A device uses an existing backed-up key; it does not replace it with a newly generated one. Offline software and any optional hardware still need verification. Sources: Decrypt · CoinDesk

title: Russia closes the exchange off-ramp
text: Access & control Russia closes the exchange off-ramp October 2026 Russia’s new digital-asset law (No. 282-FZ, in force since September 1) routes all crypto buying through licensed brokers and state-approved banks. The central bank’s October guidance is explicit: moving crypto from a regulated account to your own wallet is not permitted, and peer-to-peer trades between individuals end entirely on July 1, 2027. Small buyers are capped at roughly $3,800 a year: bitcoin, ether, or tether only. Nobody banned holding your own keys. They closed the door between the regulated system and self-custody. That door is the exact step this guide starts with, when you withdraw a test amount from an exchange to an address only you control. Why it matters here Rules can close an off-ramp at any time, in any country. A wallet built before you need it never has to ask permission. Build it while the door is open. Sources: Cointelegraph · TFTC

title: Coinbase: bribed support agents leak data on 69,461 customers
text: From the archive Coinbase: bribed support agents leak data on 69,461 customers May 2025 On May 15, 2025, Coinbase disclosed that criminals had bribed overseas customer support agents to steal customer data. The siphoning began on December 26, 2024 and was detected on May 11, 2025, when the attackers demanded a $20 million ransom. A later filing put the number at 69,461 customers, less than 1% of monthly transacting users. The stolen data included names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, the last four digits of Social Security numbers, masked bank details, government ID images, and account balances and transaction histories. Passwords, private keys, and customer funds were not taken. Coinbase refused the ransom, offered a $20 million reward for information leading to arrests, and estimated remediation and reimbursements at $180 million to $400 million. Why it matters here This is the insider version of the same lesson. The attackers did not break the cryptography. They paid the people who answer the phones. An exchange holds your name, your home address, your ID, and your transaction history in systems its own contractors can read. That data enabled phishing that tricked some customers into sending coins to scammers. Self-custody removes the coins from that database. It does not remove your identity from it, which is why the guide keeps seed material off every system tied to an exchange account. Sources: SecurityWeek · TechStory

title: FTX collapses, $8 billion in customer funds missing
text: From the archive FTX collapses, $8 billion in customer funds missing November 2022 FTX was one of the largest crypto exchanges in the world, valued at $32 billion in early 2022. On November 2, 2022, CoinDesk published the balance sheet of Alameda Research, the trading firm run by the same people, and it showed billions in FTT, a token FTX had printed itself. Customers rushed to withdraw. About $6 billion left in 72 hours, and the money was not there. FTX halted withdrawals on November 8 and filed for bankruptcy on November 11, revealing a shortfall of roughly $8 billion in customer funds. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted on seven fraud and conspiracy counts in November 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in March 2024. The bankruptcy estate later repaid most customers in dollars, but priced at November 2022 values, so a customer who had held one bitcoin got back the dollar value of a bitcoin on the day the company failed, not the bitcoin. Why it matters here An exchange balance is a claim on a company, not money in your pocket. The moment withdrawals stop, that distinction becomes the whole story. This guide keeps no balance anywhere: you buy, you withdraw a test amount to an address only you control, and you verify it before the rest follows. Even a bankruptcy that pays everyone back in dollars can still take your bitcoin. Sources: Nasdaq · Wikipedia

title: Ledger breach exposes 272,000 customer addresses
text: From the archive Ledger breach exposes 272,000 customer addresses July 2020 Ledger makes hardware wallets, and in July 2020 it disclosed that an attacker had reached its e-commerce and marketing database through a third party API key. At first Ledger said about 9,500 customers had detailed records exposed, alongside more than one million email addresses. In December 2020 the full database appeared on a public forum, and the real count was about 272,000 detailed records: names, postal addresses, and phone numbers of people who had ordered a device. No keys and no funds were touched. The damage was different: years of phishing emails and texts aimed at recovery phrases, SIM swaps, and extortion threats, all aimed at people whose home addresses were now in criminal hands. Ledger later confirmed that rogue members of its e-commerce provider’s support team had also exported customer records in April and June 2020. Why it matters here Order data is physical security data. A home address tied to a hardware wallet order tells a criminal what you own and where you keep it, and that data stays dangerous for years after the breach. Plebum Dominium works without a hardware wallet. If you later choose an optional signing device after checking your metal backups, review seller and delivery privacy and treat unexpected order messages as suspect. Sources: Ledger · CoinDesk

title: QuadrigaCX dies with its founder, $190 million locked away
text: From the archive QuadrigaCX dies with its founder, $190 million locked away January 2019 QuadrigaCX was Canada’s largest crypto exchange when its founder, Gerald Cotten, died in India in December 2018 at age 30. He alone held the passwords to the company’s cold wallets. His widow had his encrypted laptop and no password, and no one else at the company could open the wallets. About 115,000 customers were owed roughly $190 million. The exchange filed for bankruptcy in April 2019. In June 2020, Ontario’s securities regulator concluded the operation had been a fraud and a Ponzi scheme, with Cotten trading against customers under aliases. Whether the keys were truly lost or never existed, the result for customers was the same: the money was gone. Why it matters here One person holding every key is the failure this guide is built to remove. A 2-of-3 spread across three keys and three places survives any single death, loss, or theft, and the inheritance sheet exists so the people you trust can still open the fund when you cannot. Sources: CoinDesk · Wikipedia

title: Mt. Gox loses 850,000 bitcoin
text: From the archive Mt. Gox loses 850,000 bitcoin February 2014 Mt. Gox was the world’s largest bitcoin exchange, handling more than 70 percent of all bitcoin transactions in early 2014. On February 24, 2014, it suspended trading and went offline. Four days later it filed for bankruptcy in Tokyo, admitting about 850,000 bitcoin had gone missing, worth roughly $450 million at the time. About 200,000 were later recovered from an old wallet. The rest were never found. Investigations later showed the exchange had been losing coins to attackers since 2011, slowly, through flaws in how it tracked withdrawals. Creditors waited a decade: repayments through Kraken and Bitstamp began in July 2024, and the deadline for the remaining distributions runs to October 31, 2026. Why it matters here This is the original lesson of the site. Coins left on an exchange are the exchange’s coins until you withdraw them, and no reputation or size changes that. The practice spend exists so you prove the withdrawal step with a small amount before your savings ever move. Sources: The Block · Wikipedia
